He was an early artist of the Zionist movement and mixed Art Nouveau style with Jewish themes. It's a good example of how he brought together beauty and tradition.

A vase of autumn flowers sits in a swirl of rich red and golden colors. Léon Bakst used bold, glowing colors that later made his stage designs famous around the world. This picture shows the same love of color in a simple flower vase. It's a colorful decorative picture.

A young woman with a serious look is shown in the rich, graceful style of Léon Bakst, a Jewish Russian artist. Zinaida Gippius was a famous Russian poet and writer in Saint Petersburg, and Bakst painted her as part of the lively circle of artists he belonged to. The portrait shows his skill with line and color. It's a picture of a creative friendship.

paintings.t: Jacques Cartier Meeting the Indians at Stadacona, 1535
paintings.why: The French explorer Jacques Cartier meets the people of Stadacona, a village near what is now Quebec City, in 1535. Suzor-Coté painted the encounter as part of Canada's early history. The picture shows the first contact between French explorers and the Iroquoian people. It's a famous scene in Canadian history.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: A giant comet streaks across the night sky over the Mexican landscape. José María Velasco saw the Great Comet of 1882 and painted it. He was a scientist who knew a lot about astronomy. It's a beautiful picture of a real event.

A man in a hat sits and holds his rooster, a fighting cock, ready for a match. Saturnino Herrán painted the ordinary people of Mexico, including farmers and workers, as heroes. The bold shapes show his love of Mexican folk life. It's a proud portrait of a Mexican tradition.

Tom Thomson made this quick sketch for a larger painting of a river in northern Ontario, with rocks and trees in bold color. Thomson was a Canadian painter who spent summers canoeing in Algonquin Park, painting small oil sketches on wooden panels. His fresh, colorful style inspired the Group of Seven. It's a peek at how he began a painting.

Wind-bent trees and rocks stand on the shore of a bright lake, in strong, warm colors. Tom Thomson painted this wild landscape in Algonquin Park. The bold color and thick paint show his modern style. It was one of the paintings that helped make him a Canadian legend.

A wind-bent pine and a rough lake are painted quickly on a small panel. Tom Thomson made this sketch as a first draft for his masterpiece, 'The West Wind.' You can see how he worked out the wind and the waves. It's a rare look at the first idea for a great painting.

A man dressed as a confraternity member for a holy festival, with a serious face and a colorful costume. Saturnino Herrán painted the traditions of Mexican village life with respect. His paintings gave his country pride in its own faces and customs. It's an example of his last works.

A shtetl, a small Jewish town in Eastern Europe, is painted with colorful, geometric shapes. Issachar Ber Ryback was a Ukrainian-born Jewish artist who blended folk art with modern painting. He wanted to keep the memory of Jewish village life alive. It's a bright, modern picture of a vanished world.

A small figure stands in a swirling, wind-blown landscape, painted with thick, twisting strokes. Chaïm Soutine, a Jewish artist from a poor village in Belarus, used paint to express strong feelings instead of copying nature. His landscapes seem to move and twist like they are alive. He painted this in the south of France.

Soutine looks out at us with a serious, uneasy face in thick, quick brushstrokes. He came from a very poor family in a Jewish village in Belarus and was often ill and shy. His self-portraits are bold and emotional. This one is a powerful look at how an artist saw himself.

Houses seem to lean and tumble down a hillside, painted in wavy lines and rich color, as if the earth was shaking. Soutine painted this in the village of Céret in southern France. The buildings seem to dance. It's a dramatic and unforgettable landscape.

A young man with a tilted head and a dazed face is dressed in blue, painted in thick, twisting strokes. Soutine painted many portraits of kitchen workers and ordinary people, and his pictures are full of emotion. The strange title reflects an old and unkind way of describing a person who seemed different. The painting asks us to look carefully at someone others might overlook.

A woman in a dark dress looks out calmly in a quiet portrait. Martin Borgord was a Norwegian painter who lived in Norway and painted portraits and historical scenes. This portrait was painted in 1920. It's an elegant picture of a woman of the era.

paintings.t: Lady in an interior (The artist's wife)
paintings.why: A woman sits in a calm, cozy room, with soft light on her dress. Isidor Kaufmann painted his wife, who was a model for many of his pictures. He is best known for tender pictures of Jewish people in Eastern Europe, and this is a family portrait. It's a loving, quiet picture.

A boy in a white cook's uniform sits stiffly with his hands in his lap, painted in thick white and blue strokes. Soutine painted waiters, cooks and bellboys in Paris, with strong, emotional style. The wavy lines make the white clothes look almost alive. It's one of his best-known portraits.

A large rayfish hangs against a dark background with a bowl and bottles, painted with wild, swirling strokes. Soutine was inspired by famous Dutch still lifes of fish and meat but gave them a more emotional twist. The fish seems to swim in the air. It's among his famous still lifes.

Rows of tall, plain houses stand in a coal town in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, with smoke and snow. Lawren Harris, a member of the Group of Seven, painted this in 1925, using strong, simple shapes. He wanted to show the dignity of working people in Canadian life. It's an iconic painting of Canada's industrial past.

A fashionable woman in a red dress sits in a chair against a swirling background. Madeleine Castaing was a Paris patron and collector who supported Soutine and bought many of his works. Soutine painted her in bold colors with a lively brush. It's a portrait of a friend who helped him succeed.

A wooden fort sits on a hill above the North Saskatchewan River, with tents and people at its base. Paul Kane traveled across Canada in 1846–48, sketching the fur trade posts and the Indigenous peoples he met. Fort Edmonton was a major hub of the fur trade. It's an early picture of what is now a big city.

An Indigenous woman sits and weaves a blanket from wool on a simple loom. Paul Kane traveled to the Pacific coast and painted Indigenous crafts and daily life. His pictures help us see how people lived in the 1840s. It's a record of skill and tradition.

A saint kneels in a vision with a dog at his side as angels appear in the sky. Joseph Légaré was one of the first Canadian-born painters, from Quebec City. He copied European paintings and painted religious works for churches. It's an example of early Quebec art.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: A man in formal dress sits for a portrait in a calm pose. Paul Kane was a portrait painter before he made his famous journey across Canada. This early work shows his training. It's part of the story of how Kane became an artist.

A woman in a bonnet and a plain dress sits for her portrait. Paul Kane painted portraits in Ontario before his great journey to the west. The carefully painted face shows his skill. It's an early Canadian portrait.

paintings.t: Julie Papineau (née Bruneau) and her Daughter Ezilda
paintings.why: A mother and her young daughter pose in their best clothes. Antoine Plamondon was one of Quebec's most important early portrait painters, and he painted leaders and their families. Julie Papineau was the wife of a famous political leader, Louis-Joseph Papineau. It's an elegant picture of a family from French Canada.

A girl in a ruffled dress and cap sits calmly for her portrait. Antoine Plamondon, an early Canadian painter from Quebec, trained in Paris and returned to paint portraits of the middle class and religious figures. His faces are simple and honest. It's a portrait from early Canadian art.

A quiet landscape with a monument that honors General Wolfe, who died at the Battle of the Plains of Abraham in 1759. Joseph Légaré painted this in Quebec City, near the site. It is a calm picture with a big history behind it. It's an early Canadian landscape.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.t: L'Incendie du quartier Saint-Jean à Québec, vu vers l'ouest
paintings.why: A huge fire lights up the night sky over Quebec City, with people rushing through the street. Joseph Légaré witnessed the great fire of 1845 in Saint-Jean neighborhood and painted it with powerful color. It's one of Canada's earliest paintings of a disaster. It's a vivid record of the event.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: A dignified man in dark formal clothes sits for his portrait. René-Édouard Caron was a mayor of Quebec City and later a lieutenant-governor. Théophile Hamel was one of Quebec's most important portrait painters, trained in Europe in the 1840s. It's a typical example of the serious portraits that recorded the leaders of early Canada.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: A portrait of an Indigenous woman in traditional dress. Cornelius Krieghoff, a Dutch-born painter who lived in Quebec, painted many scenes of First Nations people. His pictures are an important record of life in the 1800s, though they show how a settler artist saw Indigenous people. It's a picture to study with care.

A cozy room with an officer's belongings, bed and gear, in the glow of lamplight. Cornelius Krieghoff painted this in his early years in Montreal, when many British officers lived there. It gives a close look at daily life in Canada in the 1840s. It's a charming interior.

An Indigenous hunter stands in a forest with his rifle, in a quiet pose. Cornelius Krieghoff painted First Nations people he met near Montreal and Quebec. The scene shows him in the setting of his daily life. It's part of a body of work that is important for Canadian history.

A priest in a black robe and white collar looks out with a calm, thoughtful face. Théophile Hamel painted many portraits of religious and political leaders in Quebec. His portraits are known for their lifelike faces and clear lines. It's a good example of Canadian portraiture in the 1840s.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: An Indigenous mother holds her baby in a cradleboard. Paul Kane painted this on the Pacific coast, recording how the baby's head was shaped as part of a custom. His paintings are valuable records of the customs of many peoples. It's a gentle family portrait.

Assiniboine hunters on horseback race across the plains, chasing a herd of buffalo. Paul Kane painted this on his trip across the prairies in the 1840s. The galloping horses and flying dust are full of excitement. It's one of the most famous Canadian paintings of the plains.

paintings.t: Chinook Indians in Front of Mount Hood
paintings.why: Chinook people stand in front of a huge snowy volcano, Mount Hood, on the Columbia River. Paul Kane painted this on his journey to the Pacific Northwest. The mountain towers over the scene. It's a grand landscape of a faraway place.

Two small children dig and plant in a garden, with their gardening tools. Antoine Plamondon, a Quebec painter, made this charming scene of childhood. It's one of his less formal pictures. It shows how Canadian painters also painted scenes of everyday life.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: A forest is ablaze with red, orange and gold leaves beside a calm stream. Cornelius Krieghoff painted the glorious color of Canadian autumn, which became a favorite subject. The warm colors make the picture glow. It's a good example of his love of the Canadian landscape.

A sleigh speeds away from a tollgate as the toll keeper shouts after it, in a snowy scene full of fun. Cornelius Krieghoff's lively scenes of French-Canadian country life made him one of Canada's most popular painters. It's a funny story told in a picture. It shows his eye for humor.

Anishinaabe (Chippewa) hunters track caribou through the woods and along a stream. Cornelius Krieghoff painted this to show life he'd seen in the northern wilderness. The trees and small figures show how large the land was. It's an important image of Indigenous hunting.

Two young Indigenous girls from Wendake (then called Lorette), a Huron-Wendat village near Quebec City, pose in their dresses. Théophile Hamel painted them with great sympathy and care. Many Quebec artists visited Wendake to paint portraits. It's a gentle record of the people who lived there.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: A small round painting shows a quiet river framed by trees in glowing autumn colors. Cornelius Krieghoff painted the glorious color of the Canadian fall, which became a favorite subject. The round shape makes it feel like looking through a window. It's a peaceful picture of autumn.

A bright moon shines over a rocky coast and calm sea, painting a silver path on the water. Cornelius Krieghoff painted many moonlit scenes that were popular with buyers. The mood is dreamy. It's a quiet night view.

A busy market square beside the harbor of Montreal is filled with shoppers, carts and sailing ships. William Raphael, born in Prussia, settled in Montreal and painted its streets and markets. His pictures record what the city looked like in the 1860s. It's a historic snapshot of Montreal.

People gather around a campfire in the woods at night, with the flames lighting the trees. Cornelius Krieghoff painted the glow of firelight with great skill. The picture feels warm and cozy against the dark forest. It's a favorite style of his.

People and boats gather on a harbor wharf at dusk, with the glow of sunset. Henry Sandham, a Canadian painter from Montreal, was a master of landscapes and harbor scenes. He later moved to Boston and London. It's a quiet seaside moment.

Two huge buffalo lock horns in a fierce battle on the open prairie. Frederick Arthur Verner was a Canadian painter who traveled across the Canadian west and painted the buffalo and the plains. He is known for sunset scenes of the buffalo, which he painted often. The picture captures the wild strength of the animals before their herds disappeared.

A shady forest path in dim light, painted with tall trees and soft moss. Aaron Allan Edson was a Canadian landscape painter from Quebec who loved the woods and mountains. His paintings celebrate the wilderness of eastern Canada and New England. It's a calm view of the forest.

paintings.t: A Scene in the White Mountains
paintings.why: Mountains rise above a quiet valley, with the soft light of dawn or dusk. Aaron Allan Edson painted landscapes in Quebec and the White Mountains of New Hampshire. He was part of a generation of Canadian painters who showed the beauty of the land. It's a peaceful wilderness view.

paintings.t: Ojibwa Camp, Northern Shore of Lake Huron
paintings.why: An Ojibwe camp sits on the shore of Lake Huron, with tents and canoes under a wide sky. Frederick Arthur Verner painted Indigenous people and the northern landscape. The scene records a way of life by the Great Lakes. It's an important image of 19th-century Canada.

paintings.t: A Coming Storm in the Adirondacks
paintings.why: Dark storm clouds roll over a mountain valley, with trees swaying in the wind. Homer Watson was a self-taught painter from Ontario, whom Oscar Wilde admired. He painted dramatic skies and landscapes. The painting shows nature's power.

A sailing ship glows in dim, hazy light near the harbor of Saint John, New Brunswick. Henry Sandham painted Atlantic Canada's ports and coasts in a clear, careful way. The soft light on the water gives the scene a quiet mood. It's a calm harbor view.

Woods and hills spread out in the Laurentian Mountains of Quebec, painted in rich greens and browns. Homer Watson was called Canada's greatest landscape painter of his day. He painted what he saw around him in Ontario and Quebec. It's a calm, natural scene.

A group of men stand and sit in a conference room in Quebec City in 1864, planning a new country: Canada. The painter Robert Harris created it long after the meeting, and it shows 33 delegates gathered at the Quebec Conference. It became a symbol of the birth of Canada. The original burned in a fire in 1916, and this is a copy of the lost painting.

A mother cuddles her baby in a loving embrace, with a warm and tender mood. Paul Peel was a Canadian painter from London, Ontario, who became a star in Paris. He is known for tender pictures of mothers and children. It's a sweet, gentle family picture.

A farm sits at the edge of a ravine, with trees and rolling land. Homer Watson, from Doon, Ontario, painted the farms and woods near his home. His quiet, thoughtful pictures became symbols of Canadian landscape. It's a gentle country view.

Colorful Japanese dolls and a fan are laid out together, with a bright patterned cloth. Paul Peel loved to paint beautiful objects, and Japanese goods were popular in Paris. The bright colors and rich textures are charming. It's a lovely still life.

A mother in a dark dress holds her small daughter on her lap in a quiet, tender moment at the end of the day. Paul Peel, a Canadian painter who became a star in Paris, was famous for warm pictures of home and childhood. The soft light and gentle pose make it feel cozy. It's a sweet picture of love at bedtime.
paintings.k: A mother holds her little girl. What bedtime story would you tell?

paintings.why: A sunny, dry riverbed in the oasis town of Biskra in Algeria, with a faraway ridge and a few small figures. Maurice Cullen, a Montreal painter, traveled to North Africa and painted its vivid colors. He is best known for his snowy Canadian winter scenes. It's an unusual desert view by a painter of snow.

paintings.t: John, 7th Earl of Aberdeen, Later 1st Marquess, Montreal
paintings.why: A distinguished gentleman in formal dress sits in a stately pose. Robert Harris, who was born in Wales and grew up in Prince Edward Island, was one of Canada's top portrait painters. The Earl of Aberdeen was a governor general of Canada. It's a formal portrait of a public figure.

Two girls snuggle together on a sofa over a big book, absorbed in an exciting story. Laura Muntz Lyall was a Canadian painter from Toronto who became well known for her gentle pictures of children. She painted in a soft, delicate style and exhibited in Paris and London. It's a cozy picture of reading together.

paintings.t: Labour aux premières lueurs du jour
paintings.why: A farmer with oxen plows a field at dawn, in a misty light that shines on the earth. Horatio Walker, a Canadian painter from Ontario who lived on Île d'Orléans near Quebec City, painted the farmers and animals of rural Quebec. He admired the French painter Millet. It's a noble picture of work on the land.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: Children and a woman gather nuts in a forest in autumn, in warm light. Homer Watson was known for his landscapes but occasionally included people. The picture feels peaceful and golden. It's a cozy autumn day.

paintings.t: In the shade of the apple tree
paintings.why: A young woman sits quietly in the dappled shade of an apple tree on a sunny day. Horatio Walker painted the countryside of Quebec, where he lived much of the year. The soft light and calm mood are typical of his peaceful style. It's a restful country scene.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: A portrait of a Huron-Wendat man, painted by Eugène Hamel, a Quebec artist. The Huron-Wendat have lived in the Quebec area for centuries. Painters of the time often recorded the faces of Indigenous people they knew. It's a quiet, dignified portrait.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: A stone church stands in a village in Brittany, France, painted in warm, soft colors. Emily Carr, a Canadian painter from British Columbia, studied in France in the early 1900s. She was inspired by the strong colors and shapes of French painting. It's from the years before she became known for her Pacific Coast paintings.

A dancer in a bright red dress stands with her arm raised in a flamenco pose, while a guitarist plays beside her. Clarence Gagnon, a Quebec painter, traveled widely in Europe and painted scenes from Spain. The title is the Spanish shout of praise, 'Olé!' It shows that Canadian artists also painted the world.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: People stroll and rest on a sunny beach with colorful parasols and striped beach tents at the seaside resort of Dinard in France. Clarence Gagnon painted this in his early career, when he was studying in Paris. The bright sand and sea are lively. It's a happy summer day at the beach.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: A church leader in rich robes sits in a dignified pose. Charles Huot was a well-known Quebec painter who made historical paintings and large decorations for the Quebec legislature. This portrait shows his skill with serious, formal subjects. It's an example of French-Canadian portraiture.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: A cow stands beside a fence in a soft, misty farmyard in the early morning. Horatio Walker was known as the painter of Quebec farm life, and he sold many paintings in the United States. The gentle light and quiet mood are typical of his style. It's a peaceful rural scene.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: A farmyard in Brittany, with old buildings and the glow of sunlight. Emily Carr painted this during her time in France. The bright colors show she was learning from the modern painters there. She would later bring these lessons home to Canada.

Trees in fall colors line a country lane in France. Emily Carr studied in Paris and Brittany, and learned about the bright colors of Post-Impressionism. She painted this with a bold, free brush. It shows her artistic growth before returning to Canada.

A woman in a stylish dress sits in a gentle, modern style. James Wilson Morrice was a Canadian painter who lived mostly in Paris and was friends with Matisse. He painted with soft, bright colors and simplified shapes. He's now seen as Canada's first great modern painter.

paintings.t: First Nations War Canoes in Alert Bay
paintings.why: Large carved canoes sit on the beach of Alert Bay, a First Nations village on the coast of British Columbia. Emily Carr traveled to Indigenous villages along the Pacific Coast to paint and to record carvings and village life. She wanted to preserve what she saw. It's an important record of the West Coast in the early 1900s.

A city street scene of tall buildings and giant signs, in a bold, simple style. David Milne was a Canadian painter who lived in New York and later in Ontario. He made pictures of cities, signs, and nature with clean shapes and a light touch. It's an early work from his time in New York.

A big carved canoe from the Pacific Northwest Coast, with bold shapes and strong colors. Emily Carr, a painter from Victoria, British Columbia, visited Indigenous villages to record their carvings and canoes. She was one of the first non-Indigenous artists in Canada to take this art seriously. The picture shows her respect for the beauty of what she saw.

A big wooden community house stands in the village of Ucluelet on the west coast of Vancouver Island. Emily Carr visited the village in 1912 and painted the building with bold, simple shapes. She wanted to record the Indigenous villages that were changing quickly. It's an important historical record as well as a painting.

A quiet, simple painting in dark tones, with bold shapes. David Milne painted both in New York and in the Canadian woods, always using a thin, delicate touch. He is now considered one of Canada's most important modern painters. It's an early example of his inventive style.

A small bouquet of wildflowers bursts with orange, yellow and blue against a dark background. Tom Thomson is best known for landscapes, but he also painted flowers as small sketches. The glowing colors have a joyful energy. It's a rare and cheerful still life.

A white house with a red roof stands in the sunny Caribbean, painted in a few clean, bright colors. James Wilson Morrice traveled to Cuba and the Caribbean in the winter. His light, simple style was ahead of its time. It's a sun-filled picture.

A camp in the woods is lit by the first rays of sunrise, with smoke rising from a campfire. Homer Watson painted this late in his career, with softer colors. The warm light is magic. It's a quiet and calm early morning.

Bright red and orange autumn leaves stand out against the dark woods, painted on a small panel. Tom Thomson loved the Ontario fall, when the maples blaze with color. His small sketches captured the feeling of the season. It's a vivid example of Canadian autumn.

Charred tree trunks stand on a hill after a forest fire, with new green growth rising beneath them. Tom Thomson saw the burnt land in Algonquin Park and made it the subject of a powerful sketch. Despite the damage, the spring colors show hope. It's a famous image of nature recovering.

paintings.t: Blue Lake: Sketch for "In the Northland"
paintings.why: A deep blue lake is surrounded by bright trees in a quick, colorful study. Tom Thomson made it as a first idea for his painting 'In the Northland.' The sketch is full of fresh, direct feeling. It shows how he worked outdoors, painting fast.

Boats rest by the shore of a lake in dappled light. Tom Thomson often painted on Canoe Lake in Algonquin Park, where he lived and worked as a guide. The little sketch is relaxed and bright. It's a happy picture of life on the water.

Rows of simple huts painted in camouflage patterns stand in a muddy World War I camp. Maurice Cullen was a Canadian official war artist who went to France in 1918. His paintings record what soldiers' daily lives were like. It's a quiet record of wartime.

A gray dawn light shines over a battlefield, with trenches and bare ground. Maurice Cullen painted this as an official Canadian war artist. The quiet colors seem to show both beauty and sadness. It's a thoughtful war landscape.

The ruined village of Ablain-Saint-Nazaire in France sits in rubble after the fighting of World War I. Maurice Cullen painted the ruins after Canadian troops fought near here at Vimy Ridge. The broken buildings show the cost of war. It's a record of a village changed by history.

A scene of a French town damaged by war, with broken walls and a quiet sky. Maurice Cullen painted the places where Canadian soldiers served in 1918. The painting is quiet and respectful. It's part of a series that preserves the memory of the war.

A huge crowd with flags and banners packs a Toronto street to celebrate the end of World War I. George Agnew Reid was a Canadian painter who was a leader in Toronto's art world. He painted this on the first Armistice Day in 1918 or 1919. It's a great record of public joy.

paintings.t: Forging 6-inch Shells - Cluff Ammunition Company, Toronto
paintings.why: Factory workers hammer glowing red-hot metal into shells in a busy, smoky factory. George Agnew Reid was commissioned to paint Canada's wartime work, including women and men in factories. The orange glow of the hot metal lights up the dark room. It's a record of the home front in World War I.

paintings.t: Le Pont de glace à Québec
paintings.why: People cross the frozen St. Lawrence River at Quebec on an ice bridge in winter. Clarence Gagnon loved to paint Quebec's snow, villages and winter life. In cold winters the river froze solid, and people could walk across. It's a cheerful picture of Canadian winter.
l: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec

paintings.why: Emily Carr is shown at her easel in a room with strong, simple shapes and bold colors. She was one of Canada's greatest painters, who lived much of her life in British Columbia with her pet monkey, dogs and her paintbrushes. She wasn't widely recognized until she was in her fifties, when the Group of Seven discovered her art. It's a picture of an artist at work.

Tall carved totem poles stand against a dark forest and a sky in a First Nations village in northern British Columbia. Emily Carr visited Kitwancool (Gitanyow) in 1928 and painted the poles with great power and respect. She felt she was recording a culture that deserved to be remembered. It's one of her strongest paintings of the Northwest Coast.

A still, dark pool in the forest of Temagami in northern Ontario, with trees and rocks. David Milne painted the Canadian wilderness in thin, delicate watercolors. The mirror-like pool is quiet and mysterious. It's a peaceful picture of northern Ontario.
